H_hierarchical.evidence: The paper defines four main states, then lower-level lobby/component FSMs: ΔP Measurement has Lobby1, Multi-pass enters Lobby2/TEST2 flow, Manual Control has Lobby3, and valves/pumps have their own state machines.

G_guards_arith.evidence: Multi-pass start requires a compound guard over four pumps, sensor pumps, valve A.V.2, valve B.V.12, and bypass status; valve and pump transitions add further boolean guards over valve states, pump states, levels, pressure, and delays.

A_actions_nontrivial.evidence: Starting the multi-pass test turns dirt feed into the filter test system, collects reservoir water, turns sensor pumps on, starts counters/data gathering, and later turns bypass/cleaning valves and pumps into recovery configurations.

F_fault_recovery.evidence: Route E.1 is entered from every state on emergency stop or out-of-limit parameters; automatic stop1 and safety stop2 stop pumps, interrupt measurement, and move/hold the system in recoverable manual or safe behavior.

T1_cross_section_element.evidence: Main-state behavior is in §4.5.2, valve guards/actions in §4.5.3, pump guards/actions in §4.5.4, and stop-state behavior in §4.5.5, so one supervisor behavior must be assembled across non-adjacent sections.

T2_implicit_domain_term.evidence: Although terms such as emergency stop, safety stop2, bypass, and manual control are domain terms, the paper mostly spells out the required stop, reset, pump-blocking, and valve-synchronization rules.

T3_implicit_action_from_prose.evidence: Mode entry and transition actions are described narratively, such as setting valves on measurement entry and performing multiple pump/valve/counter actions on TEST2 start or finish, rather than as a compact state-action table.

T4_multivar_arith_guard.evidence: The multi-pass start guard combines pump states, sensor pump states, valve directions, and bypass activity; bypass valves also use OR/AND-style conditions involving B.V.10/B.V.11 and pump states.

T5_composite_internal_behavior.evidence: Parent modes carry behavior beyond their substates: entering ΔP or Multi-pass initializes valves and changes HMI-visible controls/data, while component FSMs run under the mode supervisor.

T6_global_cross_cutting_recovery.evidence: The paper explicitly states that E.1 can be entered from every state, and pumps must always be turned off when automatic stop1 or safety stop2 becomes active.

C1_speculative_dfs.evidence: There are shallow composite mode entries with default lobby activation and valve initialization, but no clearly deep pseudo-state chain.

C2_expr_ir_smt.evidence: There are at least three compound guards: multi-pass start, B.V.10/B.V.11 bypass synchronization, and pump start guards over multiple valves/pumps/limits.

C3_forced_and_aspect.evidence: Global stop E.1 and automatic/safety stop rules apply across many states and pumps, making forced transitions or parent-level aspects much shorter than duplicated Umple transitions.

C4_abstract_action.evidence: Most actions are concrete pump/valve commands, but the model also describes abstract HMI status display, visual indicators, warnings, counters, and data gathering.

key_nl_quotes: E.1 can be entered from every state of the system.
Pumps can never be turned on when safety stop2 state is active.
one_line_pitch: A strong industrial HSM stress test with nested operating modes, multi-variable guards, heavy transition actions, and global stop/recovery behavior spread across supervisor, valve, pump, and safety sections.
rationale: This sample directly targets the weakest baseline areas: guarded transitions, actions, hierarchy, and fault recovery are all central rather than incidental. The paper gives enough concrete control detail to build a reference state machine, but the information is distributed across main-state, valve, pump, and inner-stop sections, which is exactly where single-prompt or syntax-repair baselines are likely to lose semantics.
